content: The available evidence does not provide a clear understanding of the impact of the intervention on healthcare service utilization, as no direct studies were identified to evaluate this outcome. Similarly, no studies were found that assessed the effects of the intervention on health behaviors, health status, or overall well-being, leaving the impact in these areas uncertain. Regarding satisfaction and acceptability, studies comparing mobile learning (mLearning) methods—either standalone or blended—with traditional learning approaches for post-registration healthcare professionals were reviewed. These mLearning methods included tools such as SMS text messages, tablet-based curricula with lecture videos, multimedia apps, audio recordings synchronized with presentation slides, daily email or RSS feed prompts, smartphone apps with didactic modules, MP3 files with heart sound audio, and tablet-based box trainers. Traditional learning methods included face-to-face lectures, one-day training sessions, textbook-based learning, conference attendance, standard didactics, and debriefing after simulated cases. The evidence on healthcare professionals' satisfaction with mLearning compared to traditional learning was of very low certainty, making it difficult to draw conclusions. Similarly, the evidence on the effects of mLearning on clinical and communication skills, as well as healthcare professionals' attitudes, was also of very low certainty. This uncertainty stems from limitations in study design, inconsistency in results, and indirectness of the evidence. In terms of cost-effectiveness, one study reported significantly lower costs per person for mLearning (via daily text messages) compared to traditional learning (a one-day workshop). However, the certainty of this evidence was very low, and further research is needed to confirm these findings. No studies were identified that reported on unintended consequences of the intervention, leaving its potential risks or negative effects unknown. The review highlights the need for high-quality trials to better understand the effects of mLearning interventions on healthcare professionals' performance, satisfaction, and clinical outcomes. The current evidence is insufficient to make robust conclusions about the effectiveness of these digital learning tools compared to traditional methods.
